title: What is Bioluminescence?
description:
BIOGLOW gets its name from living things that make their own light. It's a great hook into this season — but here's the thing to know up front: **the official challenge is about biodiversity**, not only about glowing.

> **Your season challenge:** Identify a problem that puts biodiversity at risk, and design an innovative solution that can help.

Glowing species are one of the most striking *examples* of biodiversity, and several of them are genuinely at risk — which makes them a strong starting point for your Innovation Project.

## ✨ What is bioluminescence?

Bioluminescence is light made by a living thing through a chemical reaction inside its body. A molecule called **luciferin** reacts with oxygen, helped along by an enzyme called **luciferase**, and the energy comes out as light instead of heat. That's why it's called "cold light" — a firefly's glow is nearly 100% light and almost no wasted warmth, far more efficient than a light bulb.

## 🌊 Who glows, and why

| Creature | Why it glows |
|---|---|
| **Fireflies** | Flash patterns to find a mate |
| **Anglerfish** | A glowing lure to attract prey in the deep sea |
| **Dinoflagellates** (plankton) | Flash when disturbed — startles predators, lights up waves |
| **Foxfire fungi** | Glowing mushrooms that may attract spore-spreading insects |
| **Glowworms** | Sticky glowing threads to trap insects in caves |

Most bioluminescence on Earth is in the **ocean** — the deep sea is the largest habitat on the planet, and the majority of animals down there make light.

## 🔗 Why this matters for biodiversity

Glowing species are sensitive indicators. Fireflies are declining from **light pollution**, habitat loss, and pesticides — when porch lights and streetlights wash out the dark, fireflies can't see each other's mating flashes. Fewer fireflies means fewer insects feeding local birds. A species disappearing is rarely just one species.

That's your bridge: a glowing species is a vivid, *specific*, often *local* way into a real biodiversity problem.

title: Ecosystems Where Things Glow
description:
Bioluminescence shows up in some of Earth's most amazing — and most threatened — ecosystems. Understanding WHERE things glow helps you understand WHY those ecosystems matter.

**The deep sea** — Below 1,000 meters, sunlight never reaches. It's the largest habitat on Earth, and over 75% of deep-sea animals make their own light! Threats: deep-sea mining, trawling, warming oceans.

**Bioluminescent bays** — A few rare bays (like Mosquito Bay in Puerto Rico) are so full of glowing plankton that the water lights up at night. Threats: water pollution, boat traffic, coastal development that dims the glow.

**Forests at night** — Fireflies need dark nights, moist soil, and undisturbed leaf litter. Threats: light pollution (artificial light confuses their flash signals!), pesticides, habitat loss. Firefly populations are declining worldwide.

**Caves and fungi zones** — Glow-worms in caves and glowing fungi on rotting logs depend on stable, untouched habitats.

**The big idea:** when an ecosystem gets polluted, developed, or lit up at night, the glow is often the first thing to disappear. Bioluminescence is like a health meter for these ecosystems.

## 🌱 What "biodiversity" means here

Biodiversity is the variety of life in a place — plants, animals, fungi, insects, bacteria — and how they depend on each other. It's a health signal for the planet: the more varied the life in an ecosystem, the better that ecosystem survives shocks like disease, drought, or a new predator. When species disappear, the whole web gets more fragile.

BIOGLOW is part of the larger **FIRST CANOPY** season. The big idea: scientists and engineers protect nature by observing animals, monitoring plant diversity, and building technology inspired by the natural world — and your team is going to do exactly that.

title: Hub Check: Find a Reliable Gyro
description:
Not all SPIKE hubs are equal! Some hubs have gyro sensors that **drift** — the angle reading slowly changes even when the hub is sitting perfectly still. Others measure turns badly. A bad gyro will ruin your turns and straight-line driving all season.

**Your mission:** Test at least 2 hubs with **both** tests below, then pick the best one for competition.

## 🧊 Test 1 — Drift (does it stay at zero?)

1. Place the hub flat on the table and do not touch it
2. Run the **drift test** code and watch the heading for 60 seconds
3. A good gyro stays at 0 (or flickers ±1 at most). A bad one slowly climbs: 0… 1… 2… 3…

## 🔄 Test 2 — Turning (does it measure a turn correctly?)

1. Line the hub up against a straight edge of the table
2. Run the **turn test** code — the heading shows on the hub screen so you can read it while you turn
3. Rotate the hub exactly 90° using a table corner as your guide
4. A good gyro reads **89–91**. Off by 3° or more is a bad hub
5. Press the **centre button** to zero it and repeat — do it **3 times**

**Why 3 times?** A hub that reads 90, then 87, then 93 is *unreliable*, even though the average looks perfect. Consistency matters more than one good reading.

codeExamples.label: Test 1 — Drift test (hub sits still)
codeExamples.code:
from pybricks.hubs import PrimeHub
from pybricks.parameters import Button
from pybricks.tools import wait, StopWatch

hub = PrimeHub()
hub.imu.reset_heading(0)

# DRIFT TEST - does this hub hold zero when nothing moves?
#
# 1. Put the hub flat on the table and do NOT touch it.
# 2. Start this program. The heading shows on the hub screen AND below.
# 3. Leave it completely alone for the full 60 seconds.
# 4. Read the last number.  0 or 1 = good hub.  3 or more = bad hub.
# 5. Press the CENTER button to zero it and start the 60s again.
#
# Do it 3 times and write down all 3 readings - a hub that drifts 0, then
# 4, then 1 is unreliable even though the average looks fine.

timer = StopWatch()

while timer.time() < 60000:
    heading = hub.imu.heading()
    print("Heading:", round(heading, 1))

    # the hub screen can only show -99 to 99
    if -99 < heading < 99:
        hub.display.number(int(heading))
    else:
        hub.display.char("X")

    if Button.CENTER in hub.buttons.pressed():
        hub.imu.reset_heading(0)
        timer.reset()
        print("--- reset to 0, timing again ---")
        wait(600)

    wait(200)

print("Drift after 60 seconds:", round(hub.imu.heading(), 1))

title: Motor Check: Find a Matched Pair
description:
Your drive motors are the legs of your robot. If the left motor spins even slightly faster than the right, your robot will curve when it should drive straight — and no amount of code can fully fix a bad motor pair.

**Your mission:** Test your motors and find the best-matched pair for your drive base.

**What makes a good pair:**
1. **Same speed** — when both are set to the same power, they should report nearly identical speeds
2. **Low friction** — spin each motor shaft gently by hand with no program running. It should turn smoothly with no gritty or stiff spots

**How to test:** Connect two motors to ports A and B, run the code below, and record the reported speeds. Swap motors between tests so every motor gets tested.
codeExample:
from pybricks.hubs import PrimeHub
from pybricks.pupdevices import Motor
from pybricks.parameters import Port
from pybricks.tools import wait

hub = PrimeHub()
motor_a = Motor(Port.A)
motor_b = Motor(Port.B)

# Run both motors at the same command for 3 seconds,
# then print actual measured speed of each.
motor_a.run(500)   # 500 deg/s
motor_b.run(500)
wait(3000)

print("Motor A speed:", motor_a.speed())
print("Motor B speed:", motor_b.speed())

motor_a.stop()
motor_b.stop()

title: Step 2 — Pick Your Problem
description:
Every great Innovation Project starts with a clearly defined problem. Not "pollution is bad" — that's too big. A great FLL problem is **specific, real, and affects real people or ecosystems**.

## 🎯 It has to connect to the official prompt

> **Identify a problem that puts biodiversity at risk, and design an innovative solution that can help.**

Your problem statement must make the biodiversity link obvious. A judge should read it and immediately see what living thing is at risk.

## ✍️ A strong problem statement answers

1. **WHO / WHAT** is affected? (a species, an ecosystem, a community)
2. **WHAT** exactly is the problem?
3. **WHERE** does it happen? (bonus points if it's local!)
4. **WHY** does it matter — and **why does the problem exist**?
5. **WHO** would benefit if it got solved?

**Example:** "Fireflies in our county are disappearing because streetlights and porch lights drown out their mating flashes. Fewer fireflies means fewer of the insects that feed local birds — and local kids may grow up never seeing one." — specific, local, biodiversity link is crystal clear.

## 📓 Where this goes

Write your final statement on the **Innovation Project Planning sheet (page 29)** of your Engineering Notebook. That's the page judges and your coach will look at all season.

## 🤝 Choose something everyone supports

Your team probably won't pick every member's favorite. That's normal. What matters is landing on a problem **everyone is willing to get behind** — that's the Core Value of Inclusion in action.

⏱ **Due by Session 3** — this is the deadline set by the official season guide.

title: Step 2b — Build Your Evidence File 📎
description:
You picked your problem in Step 2. Right now that is still **your opinion**. This lesson turns it into something you can defend: real numbers, real sources, and a list of real people who could tell you more.

Judges do not expect you to be scientists. They expect you to be able to say *"we know this because…"* and point at something.

## 📌 Your problem statement

One sentence, said in one breath. Use this shape until you can say it without it:

> **[Who or what]** in **[where]** is affected by **[what is happening]**, and right now **[what is missing or going wrong]**.

Example: *Fireflies in our neighborhood parks are disappearing because outdoor lighting stays on all night, and nobody in our city tracks where it is worst.*

Weak version: *Light pollution is bad for bugs.* — no who, no where, nothing you could go and check.

## 🔎 Evidence: facts with a link attached

A fact with no source is a guess. Every row in your evidence table needs somewhere it came from that a judge could open.

**Where to look:**

| Source | Good for |
|---|---|
| Government and city sites (`.gov`) | Local data, maps, regulations |
| University and museum sites (`.edu`) | Research explained for the public |
| Conservation groups (Xerces Society, Audubon, local land trusts) | Species-specific facts |
| News from your own area | What is happening *here*, and who is already working on it |
| Something your team measured or counted | Judges love this one — it is yours |

**Two rules:**
1. **Paste the actual link.** "I read it somewhere" is not evidence.
2. **Prefer a number.** "Firefly populations dropped" is weaker than "firefly counts fell by about a third in monitored sites since 2000."

## 👤 Experts you want to reach

You are not emailing anyone yet — you are building the list. Think about who would actually know:

- A professor or grad student at a nearby university
- Someone at a park, nature center, zoo, aquarium, or botanical garden
- A city employee — parks, water, sustainability, public works
- Someone at a local conservation or volunteer group
- A person directly affected by the problem — a gardener, a farmer, a neighbor

For each one, write **the actual question you would ask them.** "Tell me about fireflies" gets no reply. "We are mapping light pollution in our parks — does the city track outdoor lighting anywhere?" gets one.

## ✅ You are done when

- Your problem statement is one sentence and every word earns its place
- You have **at least five** facts, each with a link
- You have **at least three** experts with a real question written for each
- You have written down what you still do not know

## ➡️ Next

**Step 3** asks how your solution differs from what already exists. The evidence you gather here is what you will search against — so make it good now and Step 3 gets much easier.

Keep adding to this all season on your **team idea map** — it has a "What we found out" section that never closes.

title: Step 2c — Tell the Story So Far 🎤
description:
You have done a lot already: everyone brainstormed, your team narrowed it to five, and you chose one problem. Judges will ask you to walk them through exactly that — **and they care as much about how you decided as what you decided.**

This is the first time you say it out loud, start to finish. It is short on purpose: about **60 to 90 seconds**, roughly one minute of your five-minute presentation.

## 🗺️ Look at your idea map first

Open your team’s **idea map** before you write. Everything you need is on it — every idea your team had, the five you kept, and the problem you chose. You are turning that picture into sentences.

## 🎤 The script — fill in every blank

Copy this into the box below and replace everything in brackets. Keep the wording that is already there; it is doing work.

> Our team is **[team name]**, and we are solving a problem about **[your topic in three words]**.
>
> We started with **[number]** ideas. Everyone on the team brought their own — mine were **[one or two of your own ideas]**.
>
> We narrowed those down to five: **[list your five, quickly]**. We chose those five because **[what made an idea survive — real, local, doable, interesting]**.
>
> Then we picked one. We chose **[your problem]** because **[the honest reason — what made it win]**.
>
> The idea we argued about most was **[idea]**, and we let it go because **[reason]**.
>
> So the problem we are solving is: **[your problem statement from Step 2, word for word]**.

## ✅ What makes this good

| Judges like | Judges do not like |
|---|---|
| "We had 27 ideas and cut 22" — real numbers | "We brainstormed a lot" |
| Naming a teammate’s idea you backed | Only talking about your own idea |
| Saying what you gave up and why | Pretending everyone agreed instantly |
| One clear problem statement | A list of three problems you might do |
| Saying it in your own words | Reading it off the page |

## ⏱️ Say it out loud and time it

Reading in your head does not count. Read it aloud, time it, and write down what happened.

- **Over 90 seconds?** Cut the list of five down to three, and shorten your reasons.
- **Under 45 seconds?** You are missing the *why*. Judges want the reasoning, not just the result.
- **Tripping over a sentence?** That sentence is written the way you write, not the way you talk. Rewrite it the way you would say it to a friend.

## ➡️ Where this goes

This is a rough draft on purpose, and it is not wasted. In **Step 9** you write the full presentation script — this becomes the opening of it. Get it right now and Step 9 gets much shorter.

title: Step 3 — Research Existing Solutions

Judges ALWAYS ask: **"How is your solution different from what already exists?"** Teams that can't answer lose points. Teams that can answer confidently stand out.

Your mission: find out what's already being done about your problem. For each existing solution, figure out what it does well and where it falls short — that gap is where YOUR innovation lives.

**Where to look:**
- Search "[your problem] solution" and "[your problem] technology"
- Check what organizations and companies are doing
- Ask the experts you identified in your research
- Look at how OTHER countries handle the same problem

4. **Why it is better** — how it fills the gap you found in Step 3

title: Step 7 — Share, Get Feedback & Improve
description:
FLL judges give top Innovation scores to teams who **shared their solution with real people and improved it based on feedback**. This is the step most teams skip — don't be most teams!

**Who to share with:**
- An expert from your research list (email works!)
- A teacher, parent, or community member connected to the problem
- Another FLL team or your classmates

**What to ask them:**
1. "Does this solution make sense to you?"
2. "What problems do you see with it?"
3. "What would make it better?"

Then — and this is the important part — **actually change something** based on what they said, and document what you changed.

title: Step 9 — Write Your Presentation Script 🎬
description:
Deliverable #1 of 3! Your Innovation Project presentation is **5 minutes max** in front of the judges. A written script keeps you on time, makes sure nothing gets forgotten, and gives every teammate a speaking part.

**The winning 5-part structure:**
1. **The Hook (30 sec)** — grab attention! A surprising fact, a question, a mini skit
2. **The Problem (1 min)** — who, what, where, why — with your evidence
3. **Existing Solutions & The Gap (1 min)** — what's out there, and what's missing
4. **Your Solution (1.5 min)** — name it, explain it, show how it fills the gap
5. **Sharing & Impact (1 min)** — who you shared with, what you improved, what's next

**Pro tips:** every teammate speaks · practice with a timer · the hook is what judges remember — make it fun!

title: Step 10 — Build Your Presentation Slides 🖥️
description:
Deliverable #2 of 3! Slides support your script — they don't replace it. Judges should watch YOU, not read a wall of text.

**The 6-slide formula (one per script part, plus a title):**
1. **Title slide** — team name, solution name, a great image
2. **Hook slide** — one striking image or one big number
3. **Problem slide** — a photo + 3 bullet points max
4. **Existing solutions slide** — your comparison in simple visual form
5. **Solution slide** — your sketch/diagram front and center
6. **Impact slide** — who you shared with + what you changed

**Slide rules that win:**
- Max 6 words per bullet, max 3 bullets per slide
- Big images beat small text
- One idea per slide
- Practice clicking through while speaking — slides should match your script's flow

Build them in Google Slides, PowerPoint, or Canva. Paste the share link below and upload screenshots of your slides.

title: Step 11 — Create Your Team Poster 🖼️
description:
Deliverable #3 of 3! Your poster lives at your team table all competition day — judges, other teams, and visitors will read it when you're not even there. It has to tell your whole story **in 30 seconds of looking**.

Competition-ready means **no reading from paper**. Judges connect with teams who speak to them, not at a script. Time to memorize and rehearse until your presentation is smooth.

1. Read your part out loud 5 times

title: Step 1 — Brainstorm: Problems & Solution Ideas 🧠
description:
Great teams never run with their FIRST idea — they brainstorm MANY ideas and pick the best. Today there are no bad ideas: quantity beats quality, wild ideas welcome, build on each other.

## 🎯 Aim everything at the official prompt

> **Identify a problem that puts biodiversity at risk, and design an innovative solution that can help.**

So every problem on your list should finish this sentence: *"This puts biodiversity at risk because…"* If it doesn't, it's a fine idea — just not a BIOGLOW idea.

**Round 1 — Problem Storm (15 min):** List every biodiversity problem you can think of. Pull from your research, the **Project Sparks** on page 6 of your Engineering Notebook, and things you have actually seen near home. Aim for at least 5. Local problems score bonus points with judges.

Places to look for problems:
- 🐝 **Pollinators** — bees, butterflies, and the food supply that depends on them
- 🌊 **Water** — runoff, plastics, warming water, fish and amphibians
- 🌳 **Habitat loss** — building, farming, and roads splitting habitats apart
- 🦠 **Invasive species** — plants or animals crowding out natives
- 💡 **Light and noise pollution** — confusing animals that navigate by dark and quiet (this is where fireflies and other glowing species come in!)
- 🌡️ **Climate shifts** — species moving, blooming, or migrating at the wrong time

**Round 2 — Solution Storm (15 min):** Pick your 2-3 favorite problems and throw out every solution idea you can imagine — devices, apps, campaigns, new materials, nature-inspired designs. At least 5 total.

**Brainstorm rules:**
- No criticizing ideas during the storm — judge later, generate now
- Wild ideas are welcome (they often hide great ones inside)
- Build on teammates: 'yes, AND...' beats 'no, but...'
- Write everything down, even the silly ones

⏱ **Remember:** your problem statement is due by **Session 3**, so go wide today.

title: Step 4 — Choose Your Solution & Plan Your Iterations 🗺️
description:
You have a problem (Step 2), you know the gap (Step 3), and you have a pile of solution ideas (Step 1). Now: **choose your solution and plan how it will evolve**.

Real engineers never design something once — they iterate. Plan your iterations BEFORE you start so every version has a purpose:

- **Iteration 1 (v1)** — the first rough draft. Goal: get the idea on paper
- **Iteration 2 (v2)** — the improvement pass. Goal: fix what the team finds weak in v1
- **Iteration 3 (final)** — the feedback pass. Goal: improve based on what real people tell you

For each iteration, decide: what is the GOAL of this version? What will you test or question? What does success look like?

**Choosing your solution:** score your top 3 ideas from Step 1 on: Does it fill the gap? Can we explain it? Is it original (or a real improvement)? Does it excite the team?

title: What is Bioluminescence?
description:
BIOGLOW gets its name from living things that make their own light. It's a great hook into this season — but here's the thing to know up front: **the official challenge is about biodiversity**, not only about glowing.

> **Your season challenge:** Identify a problem that puts biodiversity at risk, and design an innovative solution that can help.

Glowing species are one of the most striking *examples* of biodiversity, and several of them are genuinely at risk — which makes them a strong starting point for your Innovation Project.

## ✨ What is bioluminescence?

Bioluminescence is light made by a living thing through a chemical reaction inside its body. A molecule called **luciferin** reacts with oxygen, helped along by an enzyme called **luciferase**, and the energy comes out as light instead of heat. That's why it's called "cold light" — a firefly's glow is nearly 100% light and almost no wasted warmth, far more efficient than a light bulb.

## 🌊 Who glows, and why

| Creature | Why it glows |
|---|---|
| **Fireflies** | Flash patterns to find a mate |
| **Anglerfish** | A glowing lure to attract prey in the deep sea |
| **Dinoflagellates** (plankton) | Flash when disturbed — startles predators, lights up waves |
| **Foxfire fungi** | Glowing mushrooms that may attract spore-spreading insects |
| **Glowworms** | Sticky glowing threads to trap insects in caves |

Most bioluminescence on Earth is in the **ocean** — the deep sea is the largest habitat on the planet, and the majority of animals down there make light.

## 🔗 Why this matters for biodiversity

Glowing species are sensitive indicators. Fireflies are declining from **light pollution**, habitat loss, and pesticides — when porch lights and streetlights wash out the dark, fireflies can't see each other's mating flashes. Fewer fireflies means fewer insects feeding local birds. A species disappearing is rarely just one species.

That's your bridge: a glowing species is a vivid, *specific*, often *local* way into a real biodiversity problem.

title: Ecosystems Where Things Glow
description:
Bioluminescence shows up in some of Earth's most amazing — and most threatened — ecosystems. Understanding WHERE things glow helps you understand WHY those ecosystems matter.

**The deep sea** — Below 1,000 meters, sunlight never reaches. It's the largest habitat on Earth, and over 75% of deep-sea animals make their own light! Threats: deep-sea mining, trawling, warming oceans.

**Bioluminescent bays** — A few rare bays (like Mosquito Bay in Puerto Rico) are so full of glowing plankton that the water lights up at night. Threats: water pollution, boat traffic, coastal development that dims the glow.

**Forests at night** — Fireflies need dark nights, moist soil, and undisturbed leaf litter. Threats: light pollution (artificial light confuses their flash signals!), pesticides, habitat loss. Firefly populations are declining worldwide.

**Caves and fungi zones** — Glow-worms in caves and glowing fungi on rotting logs depend on stable, untouched habitats.

**The big idea:** when an ecosystem gets polluted, developed, or lit up at night, the glow is often the first thing to disappear. Bioluminescence is like a health meter for these ecosystems.

title: Hub Check: Find a Reliable Gyro
description:
Not all SPIKE hubs are equal! Some hubs have gyro sensors that **drift** — the angle reading slowly changes even when the hub is sitting perfectly still. Others measure turns badly. A bad gyro will ruin your turns and straight-line driving all season.

**Your mission:** Test at least 2 hubs with **both** tests below, then pick the best one for competition.

## 🧊 Test 1 — Drift (does it stay at zero?)

1. Place the hub flat on the table and do not touch it
2. Run the **drift test** code and watch the heading for 60 seconds
3. A good gyro stays at 0 (or flickers ±1 at most). A bad one slowly climbs: 0… 1… 2… 3…

## 🔄 Test 2 — Turning (does it measure a turn correctly?)

1. Line the hub up against a straight edge of the table
2. Run the **turn test** code — the heading shows on the hub screen so you can read it while you turn
3. Rotate the hub exactly 90° using a table corner as your guide
4. A good gyro reads **89–91**. Off by 3° or more is a bad hub
5. Press the **centre button** to zero it and repeat — do it **3 times**

**Why 3 times?** A hub that reads 90, then 87, then 93 is *unreliable*, even though the average looks perfect. Consistency matters more than one good reading.

codeExamples.label: Test 1 — Drift test (hub sits still)
codeExamples.code:
from pybricks.hubs import PrimeHub
from pybricks.parameters import Button
from pybricks.tools import wait, StopWatch

hub = PrimeHub()
hub.imu.reset_heading(0)

# DRIFT TEST - does this hub hold zero when nothing moves?
#
# 1. Put the hub flat on the table and do NOT touch it.
# 2. Start this program. The heading shows on the hub screen AND below.
# 3. Leave it completely alone for the full 60 seconds.
# 4. Read the last number.  0 or 1 = good hub.  3 or more = bad hub.
# 5. Press the CENTER button to zero it and start the 60s again.
#
# Do it 3 times and write down all 3 readings - a hub that drifts 0, then
# 4, then 1 is unreliable even though the average looks fine.

timer = StopWatch()

while timer.time() < 60000:
    heading = hub.imu.heading()
    print("Heading:", round(heading, 1))

    # the hub screen can only show -99 to 99
    if -99 < heading < 99:
        hub.display.number(int(heading))
    else:
        hub.display.char("X")

    if Button.CENTER in hub.buttons.pressed():
        hub.imu.reset_heading(0)
        timer.reset()
        print("--- reset to 0, timing again ---")
        wait(600)

    wait(200)

print("Drift after 60 seconds:", round(hub.imu.heading(), 1))

title: Motor Check: Find a Matched Pair
description:
Your drive motors are the legs of your robot. If the left motor spins even slightly faster than the right, your robot will curve when it should drive straight — and no amount of code can fully fix a bad motor pair.

**Your mission:** Test your motors and find the best-matched pair for your drive base.

**What makes a good pair:**
1. **Same speed** — when both are set to the same power, they should report nearly identical speeds
2. **Low friction** — spin each motor shaft gently by hand with no program running. It should turn smoothly with no gritty or stiff spots

**How to test:** Connect two motors to ports A and B, run the code below, and record the reported speeds. Swap motors between tests so every motor gets tested.
codeExample:
from pybricks.hubs import PrimeHub
from pybricks.pupdevices import Motor
from pybricks.parameters import Port
from pybricks.tools import wait

hub = PrimeHub()
motor_a = Motor(Port.A)
motor_b = Motor(Port.B)

# Run both motors at the same command for 3 seconds,
# then print actual measured speed of each.
motor_a.run(500)   # 500 deg/s
motor_b.run(500)
wait(3000)

print("Motor A speed:", motor_a.speed())
print("Motor B speed:", motor_b.speed())

motor_a.stop()
motor_b.stop()

title: Step 2 — Pick Your Problem
description:

> **Identify a problem that puts biodiversity at risk, and design an innovative solution that can help.**

1. **WHO / WHAT** is affected? (a species, an ecosystem, a community)
2. **WHAT** exactly is the problem?

Write your final statement on the **Innovation Project Planning sheet (page 29)** of your Engineering Notebook. That's the page judges and your coach will look at all season.

1. **Title slide** — team name, solution name, a great image

- Big images beat small text

title: Step 1 — Brainstorm: Problems & Solution Ideas 🧠
description:
Great teams never run with their FIRST idea — they brainstorm MANY ideas and pick the best. Today there are no bad ideas: quantity beats quality, wild ideas welcome, build on each other.

## 🎯 Aim everything at the official prompt

> **Identify a problem that puts biodiversity at risk, and design an innovative solution that can help.**

So every problem on your list should finish this sentence: *"This puts biodiversity at risk because…"* If it doesn't, it's a fine idea — just not a BIOGLOW idea.

**Round 1 — Problem Storm (15 min):** List every biodiversity problem you can think of. Pull from your research, the **Project Sparks** on page 6 of your Engineering Notebook, and things you have actually seen near home. Aim for at least 5. Local problems score bonus points with judges.

Places to look for problems:
- 🐝 **Pollinators** — bees, butterflies, and the food supply that depends on them
- 🌊 **Water** — runoff, plastics, warming water, fish and amphibians
- 🌳 **Habitat loss** — building, farming, and roads splitting habitats apart
- 🦠 **Invasive species** — plants or animals crowding out natives
- 💡 **Light and noise pollution** — confusing animals that navigate by dark and quiet (this is where fireflies and other glowing species come in!)
- 🌡️ **Climate shifts** — species moving, blooming, or migrating at the wrong time

**Round 2 — Solution Storm (15 min):** Pick your 2-3 favorite problems and throw out every solution idea you can imagine — devices, apps, campaigns, new materials, nature-inspired designs. At least 5 total.

**Brainstorm rules:**
- No criticizing ideas during the storm — judge later, generate now
- Wild ideas are welcome (they often hide great ones inside)
- Build on teammates: 'yes, AND...' beats 'no, but...'
- Write everything down, even the silly ones

⏱ **Remember:** your problem statement is due by **Session 3**, so go wide today.

- **Iteration 3 (final)** — the feedback pass. Goal: improve based on what real people tell you

title: Prepare for Mission Release Day
description:
The official BIOGLOW robot game is built around mission models you construct from your **Challenge Set** and secure to the challenge mat. The best teams hit the ground running — they know how the game works before they touch a mission.

The official session plan builds your driving skills in this order, using the SPIKE app's **Competition Ready** unit:

1. **Training Camp 1 — Driving Around:** move forward, backward, and turn

Every FLL season's missions are built from the same handful of actions. Learning to spot them makes analyzing a brand-new mission fast:

- **Push / Pull** — nudge or drag an object into a scoring zone
- **Drop-off** — carry an item and release it in the right spot
- **Pick-up** — grab or lift an item from a location
- **Lift / Raise** — raise a beam, flap, or platform to a position
- **Precision** — hit a small target or stop at an exact spot

title: Mission Prototype Sketches: 3 Ideas Per Mission ✏️
description:
Before you build anything, **draw it**. Real engineers sketch several ideas before picking one — it is far cheaper to throw away a drawing than a built attachment.

## ✏️ What you have to do

For **every mission** your team plans to attempt, draw **three different prototype ideas** for how your robot could solve it. Not three copies of the same idea — three genuinely different approaches.

Then photograph each drawing and upload it here under that mission.

## 🧠 How to get three genuinely different ideas

If your three sketches all look alike, push harder. Try changing one big thing each time:

- **Different mechanism** — a pusher, a fork/lift, a hook, a scoop, a claw, a ramp
- **Different approach angle** — head-on, from the side, or on the way back from another mission
- **Different power** — passive (a fixed shape that does the work while driving) vs. active (a motor)
- **Different size** — one big attachment that does two missions vs. a small dedicated one
- **Different timing** — solve it early in the run, or combine it with a neighbouring mission

## 🖊️ What each drawing needs

1. The **mission model** it interacts with
2. The **attachment shape** — how it grabs, pushes, lifts, or drops
3. An **arrow showing the motion** — which way does it move?
4. A note on **which port or motor** it would use, if it needs one
5. Roughly **where the robot approaches from**

Pencil on paper is perfect. Neatness does not score points — clear thinking does.

## 🤔 Then pick one

Under each drawing, write what is good and bad about it. When all three are up, decide which one you will build first and say **why** in that mission's notes. Judges love hearing "we tried three ideas and chose this one because…"

## 📋 How to use this page

1. Rename each card to a real mission from the **Robot Game Rulebook**
2. In the notes line, write what that mission actually requires
3. Upload **3 drawings** per mission — the card turns green when you hit three
4. Add a card for every mission your team is attempting

> **Tip for judges:** keep these sketches in your Engineering Notebook too. Showing your rejected ideas is strong evidence of the Engineering Design Process.

title: Calibration 1 — How Far Does Your Robot Really Drive? 📏
description:
Ask your robot to drive 50 cm and it will drive… something close to 50 cm. **Close is not good enough.** Every mission depends on the robot ending up where you expected, so distance is the first thing you calibrate.

## 🤖 The robot measures itself

You do not sit there with a tape measure for this one. The program drives **every combination** of three distances (300, 500, 700 mm) and three speeds (300, 500, 700 mm/s), **twice each** — 18 runs — and prints a results table at the end:

```
requested | speed | drivebase | encoder_avg | left | right | err_mm | err_%
```

Copy those rows straight into your table below.

## 🔍 What each column tells you

| Column | What it means |
|---|---|
| **drivebase** | what Pybricks thinks it drove |
| **encoder_avg** | the two wheels averaged |
| **left / right** | each wheel on its own |
| **err_mm / err_%** | how far off it was |

**Watch the left and right columns.** If one wheel travelled noticeably further than the other, your robot is pulling to one side — that is a build problem, not a code problem.

## 📏 Then the ruler check

Here is the catch: **encoders cannot see wheel slip.** If a wheel spins without gripping, the encoder happily counts it. So the second program drives 1000 mm and you check it with a real tape measure.

If the ruler says **less** than the encoder did, your wheels are slipping — and that is the number that matters, because it is what actually happens on the mat.

## 🎯 What good looks like

- **err_% under 1%** across the table
- The **same** error at every speed (if it gets worse when faster, that is slip)
- **left and right within a few mm** of each other
- **Ruler within 1%** of the encoder

codeExamples.label: Encoder distance lab — 18 runs, prints a results table
codeExamples.code:
"""
Student Encoder Distance Test Lab

Main goal:
Compare requested straight distance vs encoder-measured distance.

This version focuses on straight driving only.
"""

from pybricks.hubs import PrimeHub
from pybricks.pupdevices import Motor
from pybricks.robotics import DriveBase
from pybricks.parameters import Port, Direction, Stop
from pybricks.tools import wait


# Robot physical constants.
WHEEL_DIAMETER_MM = 56
AXLE_TRACK_MM = 122


# Hardware setup.
hub = PrimeHub()
left_motor = Motor(Port.A, Direction.COUNTERCLOCKWISE)
right_motor = Motor(Port.E, Direction.CLOCKWISE)
RAM = Motor(Port.F)
LAM = Motor(Port.B)

robot = DriveBase(left_motor, right_motor, WHEEL_DIAMETER_MM, AXLE_TRACK_MM)
robot.use_gyro(True)


# STUDENT SETTINGS (safe to edit)
TEST_DISTANCES_MM = [300, 500, 700]
TEST_SPEEDS_MM_S = [300, 500, 700]
REPEATS_PER_TEST = 2

STRAIGHT_ACCELERATION = 400
PAUSE_BETWEEN_TESTS_MS = 1000


def reset_all():
    """Reset drivebase distance/angle and motor encoders."""
    robot.reset()
    left_motor.reset_angle(0)
    right_motor.reset_angle(0)


def encoder_mm_from_motor_angle(angle_deg):
    """Convert wheel rotation in degrees to travel distance in mm."""
    wheel_circumference_mm = 3.14159 * WHEEL_DIAMETER_MM
    return (angle_deg / 360.0) * wheel_circumference_mm


def run_one_distance_test(distance_mm, speed_mm_s):
    """Drive one straight move and return encoder-based measurements."""
    reset_all()

    robot.settings(
        straight_speed=speed_mm_s,
        straight_acceleration=STRAIGHT_ACCELERATION,
        turn_rate=400,
        turn_acceleration=300,
    )

    start_left = left_motor.angle()
    start_right = right_motor.angle()

    robot.straight(distance_mm, then=Stop.HOLD)

    end_left = left_motor.angle()
    end_right = right_motor.angle()

    left_delta_deg = end_left - start_left
    right_delta_deg = end_right - start_right

    left_mm = encoder_mm_from_motor_angle(left_delta_deg)
    right_mm = encoder_mm_from_motor_angle(right_delta_deg)
    avg_encoder_mm = (left_mm + right_mm) / 2

    drivebase_mm = robot.distance()
    error_mm = avg_encoder_mm - distance_mm

    if distance_mm != 0:
        error_percent = (error_mm / distance_mm) * 100
    else:
        error_percent = 0

    return (
        distance_mm,
        speed_mm_s,
        drivebase_mm,
        avg_encoder_mm,
        left_mm,
        right_mm,
        error_mm,
        error_percent,
    )


def print_results_table(results):
    print("\n=== ENCODER DISTANCE RESULTS ===")
    print("requested | speed | drivebase | encoder_avg | left | right | err_mm | err_%")
    print("-------------------------------------------------------------------------")

    for row in results:
        requested, speed, drivebase_mm, encoder_avg, left_mm, right_mm, err_mm, err_pct = row
        print(
            "{:<9} | {:<5} | {:<8} | {:<11} | {:<4} | {:<5} | {:+6} | {:+5.1f}".format(
                int(requested),
                int(speed),
                int(drivebase_mm),
                int(encoder_avg),
                int(left_mm),
                int(right_mm),
                int(err_mm),
                err_pct,
            )
        )


def run_all_tests():
    print("Starting encoder distance verification tests...")
    print("Goal: requested distance vs encoder measured distance")

    all_results = []

    for distance_mm in TEST_DISTANCES_MM:
        for speed_mm_s in TEST_SPEEDS_MM_S:
            for _ in range(REPEATS_PER_TEST):
                result = run_one_distance_test(distance_mm, speed_mm_s)
                all_results.append(result)
                wait(PAUSE_BETWEEN_TESTS_MS)

    print_results_table(all_results)
    print("\nDone. Smaller absolute err_mm and err_% are better.")


run_all_tests()

title: Calibration 2 — Straight & Turning at Different Speeds ⚡
description:
A fast robot that misses is worth **nothing**. A slow robot that hits every time wins matches. This lesson finds where *your* robot stops being reliable.

## ⚡ Why it matters

You get **2.5 minutes** per match, so it is tempting to run everything at full speed. Most robots lose accuracy as they speed up — especially **turning**. Your job is to find the fastest setting that is still repeatable, then use it everywhere.

## 🏁 What the program does

One program runs **both halves** and prints a table for each.

**Part 1 — straight.** Drives 500 mm at 300, 500 and 700 mm/s:

```
speed(mm/s) | measured(mm) | error(mm)
```

**Part 2 — turning.** Turns 90° at 200, 400 and 600 deg/s, reading the real angle off the gyro:

```
turn_rate(deg/s) | measured(deg) | error(deg)
```

## 🔧 You can change the settings

Near the top of the file is a **STUDENT SETTINGS** block — safe to edit:

```python
STRAIGHT_TEST_DISTANCE_MM = 500
STRAIGHT_SPEEDS = [300, 500, 700]
TURN_TEST_ANGLE_DEG = 90
TURN_SPEEDS = [200, 400, 600]
```

Found the error jumping between 500 and 700? Add a middle value like **600** and run it again to find exactly where it breaks.

## 🎯 What you are looking for

The point where the error jumps:

| Speed | Error |
|---|---|
| 300 mm/s | 2 mm |
| 500 mm/s | 4 mm |
| 700 mm/s | **23 mm** ← too fast |

That robot's competition speed is **500**, not 700. Write it down and use it in every mission program.

> **Note:** this program runs `robot.use_gyro(True)`, so turns are already gyro-corrected. If they are *still* drifting at speed, that is the wheels losing grip — no amount of code fixes that.

codeExamples.label: Speed test lab — straight and turning, prints both tables
codeExamples.code:
"""
Student Speed Test Lab

One file for testing:
1) Straight driving at different straight speeds.
2) Turning at different turn rates.

Students can edit the values in the STUDENT SETTINGS section.
"""

from pybricks.hubs import PrimeHub
from pybricks.pupdevices import Motor
from pybricks.robotics import DriveBase
from pybricks.parameters import Port, Direction, Stop
from pybricks.tools import wait


# Robot physical constants.
WHEEL_DIAMETER_MM = 56
AXLE_TRACK_MM = 122


# Hardware setup.
hub = PrimeHub()

left_motor = Motor(Port.A, Direction.COUNTERCLOCKWISE)
right_motor = Motor(Port.E, Direction.CLOCKWISE)
RAM = Motor(Port.F)
LAM = Motor(Port.B)

robot = DriveBase(left_motor, right_motor, WHEEL_DIAMETER_MM, AXLE_TRACK_MM)


# Drive settings.
robot.settings(
    straight_speed=600,
    straight_acceleration=400,
    turn_rate=400,
    turn_acceleration=300,
)


# Use gyro for better turn accuracy.
robot.use_gyro(True)


# Helper functions.
def reset():
    robot.reset()


def straight(distance_mm, then=Stop.HOLD):
    robot.straight(distance_mm, then=then)


def turn(angle_deg, then=Stop.HOLD):
    robot.turn(angle_deg, then=then)


# STUDENT SETTINGS (safe to edit)
STRAIGHT_TEST_DISTANCE_MM = 500
STRAIGHT_SPEEDS = [300, 500, 700]

TURN_TEST_ANGLE_DEG = 90
TURN_SPEEDS = [200, 400, 600]

PAUSE_BETWEEN_TESTS_MS = 1000


def run_straight_speed_tests():
    results = []
    print("\n=== STRAIGHT SPEED TESTS ===")
    print("Target distance:", STRAIGHT_TEST_DISTANCE_MM, "mm")

    for speed in STRAIGHT_SPEEDS:
        reset()
        robot.settings(
            straight_speed=speed,
            straight_acceleration=400,
            turn_rate=400,
            turn_acceleration=300,
        )

        straight(STRAIGHT_TEST_DISTANCE_MM)
        measured_distance = robot.distance()
        distance_error = measured_distance - STRAIGHT_TEST_DISTANCE_MM

        results.append((speed, measured_distance, distance_error))
        wait(PAUSE_BETWEEN_TESTS_MS)

    print("speed(mm/s) | measured(mm) | error(mm)")
    print("--------------------------------------")
    for speed, measured, error in results:
        print("{:<11} | {:<12} | {:+}".format(speed, int(measured), int(error)))


def run_turn_speed_tests():
    results = []
    print("\n=== TURN SPEED TESTS ===")
    print("Target angle:", TURN_TEST_ANGLE_DEG, "deg")

    for turn_rate in TURN_SPEEDS:
        reset()
        robot.settings(
            straight_speed=600,
            straight_acceleration=400,
            turn_rate=turn_rate,
            turn_acceleration=300,
        )

        turn(TURN_TEST_ANGLE_DEG)
        measured_heading = hub.imu.heading()
        angle_error = measured_heading - TURN_TEST_ANGLE_DEG

        results.append((turn_rate, measured_heading, angle_error))
        wait(PAUSE_BETWEEN_TESTS_MS)

    print("turn_rate(deg/s) | measured(deg) | error(deg)")
    print("----------------------------------------------")
    for turn_rate, measured, error in results:
        print("{:<16} | {:<13} | {:+}".format(turn_rate, int(measured), int(error)))


def run_all_tests():
    print("Starting speed tests...")
    run_straight_speed_tests()
    run_turn_speed_tests()
    print("\nDone. Smaller error values are better.")


run_all_tests()

title: Calibration 3 — The Square Test: Prove It Drives True 🔲
description:
This is the test that catches everything. Your robot drives a square and should finish **exactly where it started, pointing the same way**. Any error in distance or turning shows up here — because it happens **four times**.

## 🔲 Why the square is the classic test

One turn being 2° off is easy to miss. Do it four times and you are 8° off, and the robot ends up somewhere completely different. The square multiplies your errors until you can see them with your own eyes.

## 📐 What to do

1. Put the robot on tape. **Draw round its base** or mark two corners so you know exactly where it started.
2. Run the program. It drives a **200 mm**, then **400 mm**, then **600 mm** square, pausing between each.
3. After each one, measure:
   - the **gap** between where it started and where it finished
   - how far round it is **pointing** compared to the start
4. Record all three in your table.

## 🎯 How good is good?

| Gap on a 400 mm square | Verdict |
|---|---|
| Under 20 mm | Competition ready 🏆 |
| 20–50 mm | Usable, keep tuning |
| Over 50 mm | Go back to Calibration 1 |

## 🧠 Reading your results

- **Ends up short or long, but pointing the right way** → distance is off, redo Calibration 1
- **Right place-ish but pointing wrong** → turning is off, redo Calibration 2
- **Small square fine, big square bad** → your error is a *percentage*, so it grows with distance
- **Different every time** → something is loose, or your battery is low

Fix what the pattern tells you, then run it again.

codeExamples.label: Square test — 200 / 400 / 600 mm squares, prints heading error

from pybricks.hubs import PrimeHub
from pybricks.pupdevices import Motor
from pybricks.robotics import DriveBase
from pybricks.parameters import Port, Direction, Stop
from pybricks.tools import wait


# Robot physical constants.
WHEEL_DIAMETER_MM = 56
AXLE_TRACK_MM = 122


# Hardware setup.
hub = PrimeHub()
left_motor = Motor(Port.A, Direction.COUNTERCLOCKWISE)
right_motor = Motor(Port.E, Direction.CLOCKWISE)
RAM = Motor(Port.F)
LAM = Motor(Port.B)

robot = DriveBase(left_motor, right_motor, WHEEL_DIAMETER_MM, AXLE_TRACK_MM)
robot.use_gyro(True)


# THE SQUARE TEST - the real test of whether your robot drives true.
#
# The robot drives a square and should finish EXACTLY where it started,
# pointing the same way. Any error in distance or turning shows up here,
# because it gets multiplied four times.
#
# 1. Put the robot on tape. Draw around its base, or mark two corners.
# 2. Run this program. It does a small, a medium and a big square.
# 3. After each one, measure the GAP back to your mark, and read the
#    heading the program prints - that is how far round it finished.

SQUARE_SIDES_MM = [200, 400, 600]
SQUARE_SPEED_MM_S = 400
PAUSE_BETWEEN_TESTS_MS = 2000

robot.settings(
    straight_speed=SQUARE_SPEED_MM_S,
    straight_acceleration=400,
    turn_rate=200,
    turn_acceleration=300,
)

print("\n=== SQUARE TEST ===")
print("side(mm) | heading_error(deg)")
print("------------------------------")

for side in SQUARE_SIDES_MM:
    robot.reset()
    hub.imu.reset_heading(0)

    for corner in range(4):
        robot.straight(side, then=Stop.HOLD)
        robot.turn(90, then=Stop.HOLD)

    heading_error = hub.imu.heading()
    print("{:<8} | {:+}".format(side, int(heading_error)))
    print("   ^ measure the GAP back to your mark now")
    wait(PAUSE_BETWEEN_TESTS_MS)

print("\nDone. A great robot finishes within 20 mm on the 400 mm square.")

title: Calibration 4 — Tune the Simulator to Your Real Robot 🎮
description:
You already know your robot does not drive *exactly* what you ask. Now you are going to teach the **simulator** the same thing — so a path that works on screen also works on the table.

## 🤔 Why the simulator needs tuning

The simulator runs **perfect physics**. Ask for 1000 mm and it moves exactly 1000 mm. Your real robot slips a little on the mat, so it might only travel 984 mm.

Plan a mission on an untuned simulator and every single move is slightly wrong when you run it for real. Tune it once, and the simulator becomes a genuine practice table.

## 📏 Step 1 — Measure the real robot

Run the program below on your **actual robot**. It drives **1000 mm**, then turns a **full 360°**.

Long moves are used on purpose: a 2% error over 500 mm is only 10 mm and easy to miss, but over 1000 mm it is 20 mm and obvious. The full circle does the same for turning.

Write down:
- how far it **really** drove
- how far round it **really** turned

## 🎯 Step 2 — Teach the simulator

Open the **Simulator**, find the **🎯 Tune to your real robot** panel, and type in all four numbers:

| Box | What to type |
|---|---|
| Asked for (mm) | 1000 |
| Really drove (mm) | what you measured |
| Asked turn (°) | 360 |
| Really turned (°) | what you measured |

Press **Calculate trim**. The simulator works out your correction and tells you what it will do:

> *Ask the simulator for 1000 mm and it will travel 984 mm, just like your robot.*

Then press **💾 Save to my hub** so your coach can see it.

## ✅ Step 3 — Prove it worked

Run the **same** program in the simulator and on the real robot, starting from the same spot. They should now finish in **about the same place**. If they still disagree, re-measure — it is easy to read a tape measure from the wrong edge of the robot.

## 🏁 Step 4 — Now go build paths

Once it is tuned you can plan real mission routes on screen and trust them. This is the whole point: **fewer wasted runs on the real table.**

> **Coach note:** your coach can pick the best-tuned profile on your team and switch everyone's simulator to it, so the whole team plans against the same robot.

title: Step 1b — Narrow It Down: Your Team’s Best 5 🎯
description:
You each came to this with your own list. Now you turn all of those into **one team list of five**.

## 👥 Read your teammates first

Everything your team wrote in Step 1 is shown above this lesson. **Read all of it before you write anything.** You are picking the *team's* best five, not defending your own.

You will probably notice:
- The **same problem** written two or three different ways — merge those, they are one idea
- Someone spotted something you missed — that is exactly why this step exists
- One idea nobody can explain clearly — that is usually a sign it needs more research, not that it is bad

## 🎯 How to get from everything down to five

Score every idea out of 3 on each of these, then keep the top five:

| Test | Ask yourselves |
|---|---|
| **Real** | Can we name someone actually affected by this? |
| **Local** | Could we go and see it, or talk to someone about it here? |
| **Biodiversity** | Is the link to species or ecosystems obvious, not a stretch? |
| **Doable** | Could a team our size build something that helps, in our season? |
| **Interesting** | Do we actually want to spend four months on it? |

An idea that scores 15 is a strong candidate. One that scores 6 is not — even if someone loves it.

## ⚠️ Cutting an idea is not rejecting a person

The idea you have to be most honest about is your own. If yours does not make the five, say so out loud — that is Gracious Professionalism, and judges genuinely ask about how your team makes decisions.

## ➡️ Next

In **Step 2** you take these five down to one and write your problem statement. Choose carefully — this is the problem you present at competition.

title: Bench Test: Pick Your Hub & Motors BEFORE You Build 🔌
description:
Do this **before you build anything**. Every part you are about to bolt together has a personality, and two of them decide whether your robot can drive straight at all.

## 🤔 Why bench test first?

If you build the robot and *then* discover the gyro drifts or one motor is faster than the other, you have to **take it apart again**. Ten minutes on the bench now saves a rebuild later.

Plug things straight into the hub. No chassis, no wheels, nothing built.

## 🧭 Test 1 — The hub and its gyro

Two things matter:

1. **Drift** — does the heading stay at 0 when nothing is moving? A drifting gyro slowly poisons every turn you make.
2. **Response** — when you turn it 90°, does it *say* 90°? A gyro that reads 84° will be wrong on every single turn.

Test **every hub your team has** and keep the best one. Hubs genuinely differ.

## ⚙️ Test 2 — The motors

You are hunting for **two motors that behave the same**. Two things:

1. **Speed** — run both at the same speed for the same time. Did they travel the same angle? If one is faster, the robot curves.
2. **Encoders** — ask both for exactly 720°. Do they both *report* 720°, and do they agree with each other?

A pair whose encoders disagree by more than about 5° will fight each other every time you drive.

## 🎯 What you are looking for

| Test | Good | Usable | Reject |
|---|---|---|---|
| Gyro drift over 60s | 0–1° | up to 3° | over 3° |
| Gyro 90° response | within 2° | within 3° | over 3° |
| Motor speed difference | under 1% | under 2% | over 2% |
| Encoder difference | under 5° | under 10° | over 10° |

## 🏷️ Label everything

Put tape on the hub and both motors as soon as you pick them — **"DRIVE L"**, **"DRIVE R"**, **"HUB 1"**. In three weeks nobody remembers which motors were the good pair, and you do not want to run these tests twice.

## ➡️ Next

Once you have a good hub and a matched pair, go to **Design Your Base Bot** and build with the parts you just proved.

codeExamples.label: Bench Test 1 — Gyro drift and response
codeExamples.code:
"""
Bench Test 1 - Hub and Gyro

Plug the hub in. Do NOT build anything yet.
This checks the gyro drifts as little as possible and responds accurately.
"""

from pybricks.hubs import PrimeHub
from pybricks.parameters import Button
from pybricks.tools import wait, StopWatch

hub = PrimeHub()

# STUDENT SETTINGS (safe to edit)
DRIFT_SECONDS = 60
TURN_TEST_ANGLE = 90


def drift_test():
    """Hub sits still. A good gyro stays near 0."""
    print("\n=== GYRO DRIFT TEST ===")
    print("Put the hub flat on the table and do NOT touch it.")
    print("Press CENTER to start", DRIFT_SECONDS, "seconds.")
    while Button.CENTER not in hub.buttons.pressed():
        wait(50)
    wait(600)

    hub.imu.reset_heading(0)
    timer = StopWatch()

    while timer.time() < DRIFT_SECONDS * 1000:
        heading = hub.imu.heading()
        if -99 < heading < 99:
            hub.display.number(int(heading))
        wait(200)

    drift = hub.imu.heading()
    print("Drift after", DRIFT_SECONDS, "s:", round(drift, 1), "deg")
    if abs(drift) <= 1:
        print("  -> GOOD hub")
    elif abs(drift) <= 3:
        print("  -> OK, usable")
    else:
        print("  -> BAD, try another hub")
    return drift


def response_test():
    """Turn the hub by hand. A good gyro reads what you actually turned."""
    print("\n=== GYRO RESPONSE TEST ===")
    print("Line the hub up on a straight edge. Press CENTER, then turn it",
          TURN_TEST_ANGLE, "degrees.")
    while Button.CENTER not in hub.buttons.pressed():
        wait(50)
    wait(600)

    hub.imu.reset_heading(0)
    print("Turn it now. Press CENTER again when you have finished.")

    while Button.CENTER not in hub.buttons.pressed():
        heading = hub.imu.heading()
        if -99 < heading < 99:
            hub.display.number(int(heading))
        wait(100)

    measured = hub.imu.heading()
    error = measured - TURN_TEST_ANGLE
    print("You asked for:", TURN_TEST_ANGLE, "deg")
    print("Gyro measured:", round(measured, 1), "deg  (error", round(error, 1), ")")
    if abs(error) <= 2:
        print("  -> GOOD hub")
    else:
        print("  -> off by more than 2 deg, try another hub")
    return measured


drift_test()
wait(1000)
response_test()
print("\nWrite both numbers in your table, then test your next hub.")

codeExamples.label: Bench Test 2 — Motor speed and encoder match
codeExamples.code:
"""
Bench Test 2 - Motor Speed and Encoder Match

Plug TWO motors in. Do NOT build anything yet.
The goal is to find two motors that spin at the same speed AND report
the same encoder angle - those two become your drive pair.
"""

from pybricks.hubs import PrimeHub
from pybricks.pupdevices import Motor
from pybricks.parameters import Port, Direction, Button, Stop
from pybricks.tools import wait

hub = PrimeHub()

# STUDENT SETTINGS (safe to edit)
MOTOR_A = Motor(Port.A, Direction.CLOCKWISE)
MOTOR_B = Motor(Port.E, Direction.CLOCKWISE)

TEST_SPEEDS = [200, 500, 800]   # deg/s
RUN_TIME_MS = 3000
TEST_ANGLE = 720                # two full turns


def speed_test():
    """Run both motors at the same speed and compare how far each got."""
    print("\n=== MOTOR SPEED TEST ===")
    print("speed | motor A | motor B | difference")
    print("----------------------------------------")

    for speed in TEST_SPEEDS:
        MOTOR_A.reset_angle(0)
        MOTOR_B.reset_angle(0)

        MOTOR_A.run(speed)
        MOTOR_B.run(speed)
        wait(RUN_TIME_MS)
        MOTOR_A.stop()
        MOTOR_B.stop()
        wait(500)

        a = MOTOR_A.angle()
        b = MOTOR_B.angle()
        print("{:<5} | {:<7} | {:<7} | {:+}".format(speed, a, b, a - b))

    print("A difference under 1% of the angle is a good pair.")


def encoder_test():
    """Ask both motors for the SAME angle and see what they report back."""
    print("\n=== ENCODER ACCURACY TEST ===")
    print("Asking both motors for", TEST_ANGLE, "degrees")

    MOTOR_A.reset_angle(0)
    MOTOR_B.reset_angle(0)

    MOTOR_A.run_angle(400, TEST_ANGLE, then=Stop.HOLD, wait=False)
    MOTOR_B.run_angle(400, TEST_ANGLE, then=Stop.HOLD)
    wait(800)

    a = MOTOR_A.angle()
    b = MOTOR_B.angle()
    print("motor A reported:", a, " error:", a - TEST_ANGLE)
    print("motor B reported:", b, " error:", b - TEST_ANGLE)
    print("difference between the two:", a - b)

    if abs(a - b) <= 5:
        print("  -> MATCHED PAIR, use these two for driving")
    else:
        print("  -> not matched, try a different motor")


print("Press CENTER to start the motor tests")
while Button.CENTER not in hub.buttons.pressed():
    wait(50)
wait(600)

speed_test()
wait(1000)
encoder_test()
print("\nWrite the numbers in your table, then swap in the next motor.")
